writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is committed to supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across the country, including in Hamilton and Clyde Valley, ensuring they have fair access to public contracts.

Under the Procurement Act 2023, contracting authorities must now identify and mitigate barriers to SME participation in tenders; consider dividing contracts into smaller lots, (or justify any decision not to do so); and ensure mandatory 30-day payment terms are applied throughout the supply chain. Common entry barriers such as upfront insurance requirements or mandatory audited accounts have also been reduced.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, what assessment she has made of the potential merits of a single service which displays in one place, searchable by postcode or location, live (a) Met Office National Severe Weather Warnings, (b) Environment Agency flood alerts and warnings, (c) UK Health Security Agency Weather-Health Alerts and (d) recently issued Emergency Alerts, rather than members of the public having to consult each of those services separately.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The UK government works alongside partner agencies, including the Met Office, Environment Agency, UK Health Security Agency, and local resilience bodies, to provide clear and timely emergency information. Each of these existing services and alert channels is designed to fulfil a specific role and offer a distinct service, with the intention that they complement one another to form a comprehensive suite of public guidance.

Unlike traditional digital platforms or dedicated websites, Emergency Alerts do not require members of the public to actively seek out information, instead, they automatically notify individuals in an affected area when immediate protective action is required. Other channels, such as Met Office weather warnings, Environment Agency flood alerts, and UKHSA Weather-Health Alerts, provide broader, ongoing monitoring and detailed forecasts for individuals seeking comprehensive situational updates.

Government officials are actively working to improve the alignment and consistency of public messaging across all emergency warning and informing channels to ensure seamless communication during critical events. As part of this ongoing review of public warning capabilities, officials will take on board the suggestion of a single, centralised service displaying integrated emergency warnings in one searchable place.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, whether he has made an assessment of the adequacy of consumer protection law in preventing the use of AI-generated or AI-altered product images that misrepresent goods sold online; and whether he plans to issue guidance to retailers on that matter.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 prohibits unfair commercial practices, including misleading actions, that are likely to impact the average consumer’s transactional decision. This could include AI-generated or AI-altered product images that misrepresent goods sold online. Misrepresentation may be taken as an unfair trading practice and constitute an offence.

Where traders do not comply with the law, the DMCCA has strengthened enforcement powers. The Act has given the CMA new administrative powers to enable them and the courts to impose significant penalties.

There are no current plans to issue guidance to retailers on this matter.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers (DMCC) Act 2024 prohibits misleading and deceptive commercial practices that are likely to lead the average consumer to make a transactional decision, such as to buy a product, which they otherwise would not have made. This includes intentionally misleading the consumer about where the company is based. The DMCCA also clarifies that online retailers must exercise professional diligence in relation to consumer transactions promoted or made on their platforms.

Consumer law is generally enforced by local Trading Standards officers. The department regularly engages with enforcement agencies, businesses and consumer groups to understand the issues consumers are facing.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what assessment her Department has made of the risks to the resilience of the UK's communications infrastructure arising from use of privately-owned satellite internet providers; and what steps the Government is taking to mitigate any such risks.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
The UK’s public communications infrastructure operates through a competitive and diverse market and is privately owned. Satellite connectivity currently plays a small but useful role, complementing rather than replacing terrestrial networks, including by extending connectivity where terrestrial coverage is limited.

The Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021 establishes a robust security and resilience framework, requiring public telecoms providers to identify, reduce and prepare for risks to their networks and services. Ofcom is responsible for monitoring and enforcing compliance.

The Government continues to work with industry, Ofcom and security partners including the National Cyber Security Centre to assess and mitigate emerging resilience risks.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what telecommunications backup systems exist.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Telecommunications providers use a range of measures to maintain services during disruption, including battery backup at fixed and mobile network sites, standby generators, resilient network architecture, alternative routing and the deployment of temporary power and engineering support.

Providers are legally required to take appropriate and proportionate measures to identify, reduce and prepare for risks to the availability of their networks and services. Ofcom monitors and enforces these obligations and has published guidance clarifying its expectations for backup power arrangements.

For fixed telephone services, providers must offer at least one solution that enables access to emergency services for a minimum of one hour during a power cut at the customer’s premises. This must be suitable for the customer and provided free of charge to those who are at risk because they depend on their landline. Many providers offer battery backup units capable of powering broadband equipment for between four and seven hours.

Mobile operators use battery systems and generators at network sites, according to the operational requirements of their networks. If a customer’s own mobile network is unavailable, a 999 call can connect through another available mobile network, provided that another network remains operational in the area.

The Government continues to work with Ofcom and the telecommunications and electricity sectors to strengthen coordination, improve the restoration of affected services and support the resilience of the United Kingdom’s communications networks.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of reports that automated software, including AI agents, now account for the majority of web traffic; and what implications this has for the security and resilience of UK online services.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the growing role of automated software in online activity and is assessing the implications for the security and resilience of UK online services. Advances in AI and automation have the potential to increase the speed and scale of cyber activity, including vulnerability discovery, reconnaissance and exploitation. We continue to encourage organisations to strengthen their resilience through effective vulnerability management, secure service design, strong authentication and appropriate monitoring. These measures help protect online services against evolving threats, including those enabled by greater levels of automation.

More broadly, we are taking a range of actions to strengthen UK cyber resilience. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, currently making its way through Parliament, will strengthen the security and resilience of our essential and digital services. The Autumn Budget announced £60 million for Cyber Shield to use agentic AI to improve cyber defences, £70 million for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre to identify cyber vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and £40 million for a National Agentic Security Unit to develop new capabilities to detect, investigate and respond to agentic AI incidents.

We are also supporting SMEs to strengthen their cyber security, including through a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification and tailored advice through the Cyber Action Toolkit. Later this year we will publish the National Cyber Action Plan setting out further steps we will take with industry to improve UK cyber resilience.

The Government is working closely with regulators and industry to support the safe and responsible use of AI agents in financial services. This includes developing approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution, and considering whether further work is needed as the use of agentic AI develops.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what guidance her Department provides to local authorities on the recovery of unspent Direct Payments from families of disabled children who have been unable to recruit a Personal Assistant for the full period funded.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Under Section 17A of the Children Act 1989, local authorities may make direct payments to enable families of disabled children to arrange services to meet their assessed needs.

The Community Care, Services for Carers and Children's Services (Direct Payments) (England) Regulations 2009 set out the circumstances in which local authorities may recover these payments.

Specifically, Regulation 15 provides that a local authority may require repayment where it is satisfied that a direct payment has not been used to secure the service for which it was intended, or where specified conditions have not been complied with.

The legislation therefore provides local authorities with discretion rather than requiring automatic recovery of unspent funds. Where families have been unable to recruit a personal assistant, the department considers it reasonable for local authorities to take account of individual circumstances when exercising this discretion, alongside their continuing responsibilities to meet children's assessed needs.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what steps her Department is taking to ensure that teachers receive adequate, age-specific guidance to distinguish between types of harmful sexual behaviour (as defined by KCSIE 2026) ranging from developmentally expected behaviour to abusive or violent behaviour when the children involved are as young as primary-school age.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
‘Keeping children safe in education’ provides the statutory safeguarding framework for schools and colleges, including primary schools, supporting staff to identify concerns, take timely action and protect children from harm. Part five provides clear guidance on harmful sexual behaviour and how to distinguish developmentally expected sexual behaviour from inappropriate, problematic, abusive or violent behaviour. The guidance signposts to additional sources of advice on stages of typical sexual development and behaviour for different age groups. It also emphasises the importance of the designated safeguarding lead having a good understanding of harmful sexual behaviour.

Our revised relationships, sex and health education guidance complements this assessment framework through age- and stage-appropriate teaching about boundaries, privacy, appropriate and inappropriate contact, and recognising abuse. It also states that staff should be trained in safeguarding and supporting pupils. These curriculum and training expectations support prevention and reporting. They do not replace individual safeguarding assessment.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what assessment she has made of the progress achieved by Devon County Council under the improvement arrangements established following its May 2022 local area SEND inspection.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Devon local area partnership’s special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) re-visit in May 2022 found that insufficient progress had been made against the four areas of significant weakness identified during their full SEND inspection in December 2018.

In September 2022, the department issued Devon County Council with an improvement notice, and required the council to develop an Accelerated Progress Plan (APP), to drive progress against the four areas of significant weakness. Since 2022, the department and NHS England have assessed the local area partnership’s progress against its APP through regular monitoring reviews.

The department’s latest review in September 2026 found that the partnership was taking positive steps to improve SEND services in Devon. The review found an improved understanding across the partnership of the strengths and weaknesses of SEND services while recognising that further progress is needed to secure consistently better experiences and outcomes for children and young people with SEND.

Ofsted and the Care Quality Commission inspected the partnership in October 2026. The report is expected in December. Following publication of the report, the department will consider the findings and review its monitoring and oversight arrangements in line with its established policies and procedures.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what social security-related data sharing agreements are in place between the Department for Work and Pensions and a) the Welsh Government and b) local authorities in Wales.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As a public sector body, DWP requires both a legal power and a lawful basis to share personal data in accordance with the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018.

DWP routinely shares data with other government departments, devolved governments and local authorities (LAs) across the UK.

DWP currently shares data with the Welsh Government for purposes including:

  • Get Britain Working Trailblazer
  • Family Resources Survey (FRS) and Households Below Average Income (HBAI) statistics
  • Wales Skills Employment Pathway
  • Careers Wales

Data sharing with Welsh councils and local authorities include:

  • Pembrokeshire County Council: Local Supported Employment
  • Cardiff Council: Local Supported Employment
  • South West Wales, Mid Wales: Connect to Work
  • South West Wales, Denbighshire, Powys and Cardiff: Connect to Work Phase 2
  • Neath Port Talbot: Get Britain Working Trailblazer

Operationally, DWP has a significant number of data-sharing arrangements with local authorities, with personal data flowing in both directions. At a national level, these include, but are not limited to:

  • Access to DWP systems: LAs have access to DWP's Customer Information System for a range of purposes, including local benefit administration and local welfare provision.
  • Access to HMRC PAYE data: DWP provides LAs with access to HMRC PAYE data for several purposes, including Housing Benefit, Local Council Tax Reduction and Adult Social Care Financial Assessments.
  • Daily data files: DWP provides a range of daily bulk files notifying LAs of relevant changes to DWP benefits and HMRC PAYE income for citizens in whom the LA has an interest.
  • Fraud and error data: DWP shares monthly files with LAs identifying data discrepancies that could indicate fraud or error in Housing Benefit claims.
  • Housing Benefit administration data: LAs provide DWP with data relating to their administration of Housing Benefit.

At the Jobcentre level, there are also numerous smaller, locally managed data-sharing arrangements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what criteria their Department uses to determine whether a contractor has experienced a critical performance failure in the delivery of services under its contracts.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Department assesses contractor performance against clear contractual requirements tailored to the nature, complexity and risks of each contract. Contracts cover a diverse range of goods and services and, as part of the procurement and contract management process, appropriate key performance indicators (KPIs), service levels and performance thresholds are established to reflect the specific requirements and risks of each contract.

Contractor performance is monitored against these contractual requirements. Where performance falls below the required standards, action is taken in accordance with the terms of the individual contract. In determining the seriousness of a failure, the Department considers factors such as the nature, severity and material impact of the performance issue on contract delivery.

Depending on the circumstances, contractual remedies may range from performance improvement measures and formal notices through to service credits, other contractual remedies, or termination for breach in cases of serious contractual failure.

The criteria applied within individual contracts are consistent with the relevant legislative framework, including the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 and the Procurement Act 2023, which contain provisions relating to supplier performance and poor performance in public procurement.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they are taking to prevent cyber-attacks on refrigeration systems used for the storage of medicines, blood plasma and vaccines; and to mitigate the effects of any such attacks.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Individual organisations remain responsible for the procurement of medical devices. As part of the procurement, risk assessments of equipment are carried out in accordance with NHS England’s Guidance on protecting connected medical devices, published in October 2022.

The Cyber Security Strategy for Health and Care to 2030, published in March 2023, sets out a vision for a cyber resilient health and care sector, including focusing on the greatest risks and harms. Through the mandatory Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT), we set a cyber security standard for NHS organisations proportionate to their risk profile.

Implementation of these guidelines and standards are monitored through the mandatory DSPT which is independently audited for NHS trusts. To further strengthen the resilience of the NHS critical supply chain, the Cyber Security Supply Chain Charter allows current and future suppliers to pledge to be a trusted partner to the health and care system.

Adherence to all these standards help organisations to ensure that their networks are secure and that risks with associated Internet-of-Things medical devices are suitably understood and mitigated. Following the recent attacks on refrigeration systems, further specific advice has been shared with NHS organisations on the Threat Intelligent Sharing Platform detailing the threat, and reinforcing guidance on how to protect connected medical devices.

Whenever cyber-incidents do occur, NHS England provides a suite of support to help organisations recover quickly, but safely. This includes specialist, on the ground, certified incident response services free of charge to NHS organisations who have been severely impacted by cyber incidents as well as technical and operational support to contain, investigate, and remediate incidents.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, whether she will assess the potential merits of requiring pubs, bars and nightclubs to install CCTV in corridors and stairwells leading to toilet facilities in order to help prevent spiking incidents and to support police investigations.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Spiking is an appalling crime that undermines the public's right to feel safe whether they are out and about or in their own home.

Under Section 182 of the Licensing Act (2003), Licensing authorities have powers to attach conditions to premises’ licences to reduce the risk of spiking and support potential victims, such as the installation of CCTV. We are committed to ensuring that the licensing regime remains proportionate and continues to promote the licensing objectives relating to public safety, crime and disorder while also supporting responsible businesses to grow and thrive.

The Government is taking a range of actions to increase awareness of spiking and reduce its occurrence through a combination of prevention, education, enforcement and victim support. This includes introducing a new offence for spiking through the Crime and Policing Act 2026, expected to come into force in spring 2027. We have also funded new guidance and training for police officers, provided free specialist training for hospitality sector staff, and commissioned academic research into perpetrator motivations. We also funded Project Alliance, piloting new police sample collection kits and alternative routes for victims to provide timely samples for laboratory testing.

We continue to work with licensing authorities, police, and the hospitality sector to promote these powers, share good practice and make venues safer.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government, under the changes announced in the update to A Fairer Pathway to Settlement on 2 November, on what basis the new rules will be applied retrospectively to those who were not on safe and legal routes who have already been granted refugee status and are still on the five-year pathway to settlement; what is their assessment of the numbers who will be affected; whether the penalty for arriving by an irregular route will also be applied retrospectively; and whether there will be any transitional protection for those who are close to accessing indefinite leave to remain.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, the Home Secretary announced the Government's final approach to earned settlement, following a 12-week public consultation which received more than 200,000 responses. The new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

Successive governments have always retained the ability to change the Immigration Rules. The courts have recognised that, unless transitional provisions are made, applications are ordinarily considered under the Immigration Rules in force at the date of settlement decision. Being in the UK does not give someone an automatic right to settle under the rules that existed when they first arrived.

The Government has listened carefully to concerns about how the Earned Settlement reforms should apply to people already living in the UK and has refined the reforms in response.

Refugees will continue to receive protection where they need it, while settlement will reflect how they came to the UK, how they have contributed and integrated after arrival, and whether they have complied with the rules. A different approach will apply to people granted protection following an asylum claim made after entering the UK outside of a Safe and Legal route.

Anyone who enters the UK illegally will ordinarily face an additional 10 years waiting period before becoming eligible for settlement, regardless of the immigration route on which they seek to settle. The additional 10 years will not apply where an individual is protected by Article 31 of the Refugee Convention, which provides protection from penalties for illegal entry for refugees who meet specified conditions, including that they have come directly to the UK. Further detail on how this safeguard will operate will be set out before implementation.

Those refugees, not on Safe and Legal routes, who claimed asylum before 2 March 2026 will move to Core Protection. Any time spent with refugee status will count towards settlement.

We remain committed to publishing economic and equality impact assessments ahead of implementation. We will also publish further guidance setting out additional technical and operational detail, informed by continued engagement with affected groups and stakeholders.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what plans they have to work with technology providers to counter online finance, romance, and other scams defrauding UK users.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
We are deeply concerned by the devastating financial and emotional impact that fraud can have. Data suggests that at least 56% of all UK frauds originate online, and the Government takes this issue very seriously. All platforms have a responsibility to ensure their platforms are not used as a vector for fraudulent activity.

The Online Safety Act is now in place. Since March 2025, online platforms and services are required to do more to stop fraudulent content, of all fraud types, from reaching potential victims. From 2027, this will also include additional measures for the largest platforms to tackle fraudulent adverts, which are commonly used to push fraudulent financial promotions. Failure to comply will result in huge fines for companies from Ofcom.

However, we recognise that more can be done. In March this year, we published a new Fraud Strategy setting out our approach to disrupt the tools, methods and systems exploited by criminals to commit online fraud. This includes exploring vulnerabilities in marketplace listings, and through fraudulent online adverts. It also details how law enforcement will work with industry, including the digital platforms, to identify and disrupt criminal networks. The Strategy can be viewed in full here: Fraud Strategy 2026 to 2029 - GOV.UK.

We will continue to work closely with technology companies to ensure UK users are protected from online fraud.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the safety of military bases in the United Kingdom; and whether they are secure from attacks by Iran and Russia.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
We keep the security of military bases under constant review. Defence uses a layered, risk-based approach that combines physical protection, access controls, policing and guarding, surveillance, monitoring and counter-drone capabilities which can identify and facilitate the capture of drones, rather than relying on any single measure.

Following recent security incidents, we have maintained enhanced vigilance across the Defence estate and strengthened protective measures where necessary. Sites have been directed to review their security posture and reinforce existing measures, focusing particularly on critical assets, known vulnerabilities and operationally important locations.

We are also investing in longer-term improvements. The Defence Investment Plan allocates an additional £470 million over four years to improve site protection through better security technology and infrastructure. Alongside Defence’s investment in surveillance and counter-drone capabilities, the Plan provides over £750 million to strengthen short-range counter-drone protection for the UK and deployed forces. Work is also underway to extend Restricted Airspace protections around Defence sites.

Recent arrests demonstrate that those who seek to compromise the security of Defence sites can expect a robust security and police response. Where criminal offences are suspected, we won't hesitate to use the full range of powers available, including the National Security Act.
writtenQuestions.heading: Military Bases: Security

writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Justice
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Legal services regulation is independent of government, and it is primarily for the independent legal services regulators to ensure that legal professionals comply with their existing professional and ethical obligations, including when using AI. Legal professionals remain accountable for the services they provide, irrespective of the technology used. As such, the Government does not have any plans to restrict the use of AI in the delivery of legal services.

The Ministry of Justice is working with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and legal services regulators through the Advisory AI Growth Lab, launched in June 2026, to provide greater clarity on how existing regulatory requirements apply to AI and support its responsible adoption in the sector.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, pursuant to the Answer of 3 November 2026 to Question 39175 on Electric Vehicles: Excise Duties, whether the eVED Connect system will be technically capable of accessing (a) vehicle location data, (b) journey routes and (c) the time and date of individual journeys; and what plans his Department has for the collection and retention of such data by HM Revenue and Customs.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As answered in the previous PQ (39175) the Government is developing eVED Connect as an optional additional service, which will allow motorists to choose to use their vehicle’s own in-built connectivity to automate mileage reporting. The detailed design of the service is still being developed, and the Government will continue to work with vehicle manufacturers and other stakeholders as this work progresses.

However, the Government is committed to protecting motorists’ privacy which will be central to the design of eVED Connect. Therefore, any future use of vehicle connectivity will be optional and the data collected for the administration of eVED Connect will only be applicable to those who enter into the optional service. There will be no requirement to report where or when miles are driven, or to install trackers in cars within eVED Connect.

eVED will be administered by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA).

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what assessment he has made of the risks of technical and operational dependency on Atos in relation to National Savings and Investments’ core retail-savings systems and services; and what exit planning and assessment of the potential merits of insourcing of those systems has been undertaken.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As part of its transformation programme, NS&I is moving away from working with a single supplier, Atos, to give it greater flexibility to make sourcing decisions and change suppliers. As set out in its recent Programme Business Case, this programme will enable NS&I to improve business performance, operational resilience, value for money and innovation. As part of this, in April 2025, Sopra Steria Ltd took over responsibility for certain parts of NS&I’s operations from Atos.

NS&I is also increasing its inhouse capability in key areas that are vital to run its business, hold suppliers to account, prevent it from becoming overly dependent on a supplier, and widen its sourcing choices in the future. NS&I will continue to review and iterate the approach in line with the Government’s new Public Interest Test on Insourcing – more information on this is available here: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-024-the-public-interest-test-and-insourcing-strategy/ppn-024-the-public-interest-test-and-insourcing-strategy-html

writtenQuestions.answerText:

HMRC has assessed the expected impacts on taxpayers joining MTD for Income Tax, including the administrative burden on businesses, for those already mandated and for future cohorts. These assessments take account of the time and costs involved in preparing for and operating MTD, which will vary depending on factors such as the size and complexity of the business and its existing digital capability.
